newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-PLAYERS, MANAGERS LOOK FORWARD TO INTER-LEAGUE GAMES.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-PLAYERS, MANAGERS LOOK FORWARD TO INTER-LEAGUE GAMES.

text.p: Baseball purists may never accept it, but players and managers appear to be looking forward to the change of pace when regular-season inter-league games take place for the first time beginning on Thursday.

The experiment begins with a quartet of American League West Division teams facing counterparts from the National League West in games that will count -- a total departure from history and tradition that has only had teams from the two leagues hooking up in the World Series.

"It's great, the fans will love seeing different players they never see and we get to go to more cities and see new ballparks," said Seattle Mariners superstar Ken Griffey Jr., whose team will host the Colorado Rockies Thursday.

In the other three series that begin inter-league play, the Texas Rangers host the San Francisco Giants, the Los Angeles Dodgers travel to Oakland to play the Athletics and the Anaheim Angels play host to the San Diego Padres.
"It's good for business and it perks up interest in the middle of the season," said Seattle manager Lou Piniella. "I like it."

One of the more intriguing inter-league matchups on the schedule will be a rematch of last year's World Series between the New York Yankees and Atlanta Braves -- a series in which the Braves will be looking to exact some revenge.
"There will be an electricity when we play the Yankees because of losing to them in the World Series. We consider them rivals," said Atlanta's Chipper Jones.
"We are the dominant National league team this year and the Yankees are the defending world champions."
Jones's teammate, pitcher Denny Neagle, was also looking forward to the rematch. And to help get the AL-NL rivalry off the ground, Neagle took a swipe at one of the other American League clubs.

"We are going to face the New York Yankees in New York. I think it's good for baseball," Neagle said. "I think, obviously, it will be good for attendance. If you are a Yankee fan who would you rather see, the Atlanta Braves or the Minnesota Twins."
In all, a total of 214 inter-league matches are scheduled in the break from tradition that was agreed to as part of baseball's most recent collective bargaining agreement.
Of particular interest will be the contests between local teams whose fans have long considered themselves rivals, even though the clubs never meet in games that count.

The New York Yankees will play the New York Mets, Chicago's White Sox and Cubs will meet and the San Francisco Giants will face the nearby Oakland Athletics in a matchup that has only previously taken place in a World Series.

"I want to play the Yankees. It's been a rivalry that was never talked about for a long time," noted Mets manager Bobby Valentine. "If we could take two out of three from them, what a shot in the arm for our fans."

"As a manager it's just another game you have to win, but as a child of New York I understand how the fans feel," said Yankees skipper Joe Torre, whose club plays its first inter-league game Friday against the Florida Marlins.
Added Giants manager Dusty Baker: "There is a rivalry that goes beyond just inter-city teams. It's between the leagues.
"With that many games we might find out who the better league is."

To be sure, there are differences between the leagues with the most obvious being that pichers in the NL must take their turn at bat while the AL uses a designated hitter in the lineup. Like the World Series, pitchers will have to hit in inter-league games that take place in National Legue cities.
"It's going to be interesting," said Phil Garner, manager of the AL Milwaukee Brewers, who played for the Pittsburgh Pirates in the NL.
"I spent a lof of years in the National League and they have their style, it's different than ours," Garner said.
"We are going to Chicago to play the Cubs first. I hope our pitchers have been taking a lot of batting practice and are ready to hit."
Of course, not everyone was looking forward to this new wrinkle without reservation.
Tigers manager Buddy Bell was concerned about his pitchers facing pitching, in some cases for the first time in their careers. "I hope no one gets hurt," Bell said.
And then there was Atlanta pitcher Tom Glavine echoing the lament of the purists who worry that all the inter-league play will dilute interest in the traditional meetings between the leagues.
"I hope it doesn't take away froma the All-Star Game and the World Series," he said.
